endorsements.quote: These interdisciplinary AI working groups should also have a balanced representation from other domains, including academics from both STEM fields and humanities, industry professionals from informatics and data science, regulatory bodies, administrative leadership, and patients or their advocates if applicable.

Additionally, nurse scientists can conduct ongoing community engagement, including educational sessions and patient-family dialogs, disseminate op-eds and hold discussion groups on social media platforms to explain how AI tools inform care decisions and to gather feedback that informs iterative redesign.

Additionally, academic institutions must prepare the future generations of nurse scientists and interdisciplinary partners for effective collaboration in AI research.

To ensure that such training is adopted consistently and widely across institutions, we urge the development of a set of AI-in-nursing competencies that can guide the design of educational curricula and courses regarding AI.

Nurse scientists can work on embedding transparency mechanisms (e.g., model cards, plain-language summaries, and data provenance documentation) into all research and clinical AI applications so patients, families, and clinicians can clearly understand what the AI does and does not do.

Nurse scientists have a key role to ensure that AI systems used for nursing assessments and care delivery among patients and families are adopted only following comprehensive assessments of their clinical, ethical, social implications.

Nurse scientist–led financial evaluation further differs from generic AI integration efforts by explicitly modeling costs and benefits at the level of nursing work, including time-on-task, staffing mix, surveillance burden, moral distress, training load, and impacts on care continuity—dimensions that are rarely captured in institutional ROI calculations.

unlisted_practices: Develop a dedicated clinical AI nursing role responsible for stewardship, validation literacy, drift surveillance, and risk communication.
Create new funding mechanisms and incentive structures that keep pace with the rapid speed of AI development.
Conduct comprehensive economic analyses (total cost of ownership and ROI) of AI before, during, and after implementation.
Expand nurse scientists' participation in interdisciplinary AI working groups on development, design, deployment, evaluation, and policy-making.
Integrate AI literacy and AI design and evaluation content into graduate nursing education and expand AACN Essentials Domain 8.
Research and develop new informed-consent models for AI use and secondary data use, since current opt-out protocols may be insufficient.
Sustain bidirectional academic-industry partnerships that embed nurse scientists as co-architects in AI problem formulation, validation, and deployment.
Preserve clinician autonomy and accountability in AI-influenced clinical decisions and avoid marketing AI tools as "AI nurse" or "robot nurse".
Report data representativeness, bias, and algorithm integrity issues alongside findings of AI-based research.
